transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, thank you for seeing me, doctor. I, uh, I guess what really brings me in today is... well, it’s this feeling lately that I’m just constantly running on a motor. I mean, I’m 58 years old, you’d think a guy my age would be slowing down a bit, taking it easy, but it’s the exact opposite. It’s like I have this engine inside me that’s just revving, all day, every day, and someone cut the brake lines. 

I’m a special education teacher, and you know, that’s a demanding job on its own. There’s always a situation to de-escalate, or an IEP meeting, or a lesson plan to adjust, but it’s not just the environment. It’s me. I’ll finish one thing at school—like, say I just finished getting my classroom’s sensory stations set up for the morning—and I immediately jump right into the next thing without even taking a breath. I'm pacing the halls, checking on other teachers, rearranging the desks. Just go, go, go. 

And then I get home, and you’d think I’d sit down in my recliner and watch the news, but no, I walk through the front door and immediately start cleaning the gutters, or I'm pulling everything out of the garage to reorganize the tool bench for the third time this month. I just bounce from one task to the next, at work and at home, and I can never seem to just... shut myself off, you know? It’s honestly exhausting, never being able to power down, but I just can't stop.
Do you often feel restless when you're not actively doing something?

Oh, absolutely. Restless doesn't even begin to cover it. If I'm forced to just sit there and not actively work on something, it's almost like physical torture. 

Take IEP meetings, for example. As a special ed teacher, I'm in those all the time. You've got the parents, the school psychologist, maybe the principal or a district rep, everyone sitting around this big conference table for an hour or more, and it's supposed to be this very serious, focused environment. But I just... I can't just sit there. Underneath the table, my leg is going a mile a minute, just bouncing, bouncing, bouncing. And if it's not my leg, I've got a pen in my hand and I'm clicking it, or I'm shifting my weight from one side of the chair to the other, crossing and uncrossing my arms. 

I'm taking some administration classes right now, too, trying to keep my credentials up to date, and it's the exact same thing there. I'll be sitting in the lecture, trying to listen to whatever policy they're talking about, and I'm just squirming in my seat. The worst part is, I don't even realize I'm doing it half the time. It's completely unconscious until I notice the person next to me giving me this look, you know? They glance over at me, or they stare at my hand, and suddenly I realize I've been clicking my pen like a madman or shaking the whole table with my knee for the last ten minutes. 

It's embarrassing, frankly. I'm a 58-year-old professional, I should be able to sit through a standard meeting without fidgeting like one of my middle schoolers, but I just have this pent-up energy that absolutely has to leak out somehow if I'm not up on my feet moving around. I try to stop, I really do, I'll put my hands flat on the table, but two minutes later, I'm tapping my fingers or shifting around all over again.
Do you often find it difficult to focus on what's being said or to follow through on instructions?

Well, no, not really. I mean, I hear what people are saying just fine. When I'm in those IEP meetings, even if my leg is bouncing or I'm shifting around, I'm still tracking the conversation. I'm listening to the parents, I'm taking in what the school psychologist is suggesting about accommodations. I don't really lose the thread of the conversation, you know? 

And as far as instructions go... well, in my job, I'm usually the one giving them, but even when I'm taking those administration classes I mentioned, I don't have trouble understanding what the professor wants us to do for an assignment. If they say we need to write a ten-page paper on district policy changes, I hear it, I know what I need to do, and I get it done. The problem isn't that I can't focus on what's being asked of me, or that I get confused and forget the steps. It's more just... the physical act of sitting there while the instructions are being given. 

Like, last week, my wife asked me to help her put together this new shelving unit for the garage. She was reading the manual, telling me which brackets go where, and I understood her perfectly. I didn't miss a word. But while she was reading, I was already grabbing the drill, pacing around the boxes, sorting the screws, just itching to get my hands on it and start building. I wasn't distracted from what she was saying, I was just... impatient to be doing it. So, no, I wouldn't say I have a hard time focusing on people or following through. It's just the sitting still part that gets me.
Do you often act on impulse without thinking through the consequences?

Well, no, not really. I mean, I wouldn't say I'm impulsive in a dangerous or reckless way, like, you know, gambling away the mortgage or buying a sports car on a whim. I'm a planner by nature, especially with my job. You have to be. You can't just wing an IEP for a student with severe behavioral needs, you know? You have to think through every possible scenario, every trigger, every accommodation. And I do that. I'm very thorough. 

So, I don't just act without thinking about the big things. Like with those administration classes I'm taking. I didn't just wake up one morning and decide to enroll. I looked at the district requirements, I talked to my principal about potential career paths, I figured out the tuition costs and how it would fit into my schedule. I mapped the whole thing out. 

I guess... maybe I can be a little quick to jump into action, like I was saying about the garage shelves with my wife. I just want to get things moving. If there's a problem, I want to fix it right that second. If one of my students is having a meltdown, I'm right in there, intervening, trying to de-escalate before anyone else even realizes what's happening. But I wouldn't call that acting without thinking of the consequences. I'm thinking of the consequences, I'm just trying to prevent them from getting worse by acting fast. I'm just... I'm a doer. I don't sit back and wait for things to happen, but I'm not reckless about it. I've been doing this a long time, 58 years, and I've always been this way. I just like to keep things moving forward. So, no, I wouldn't say I have a problem with impulse control or ignoring consequences.
Has your constant need to be active and moving ever caused problems at work or in your relationships with others?

Well, yes. Yes, it has, and it's... it's actually become quite a serious issue lately, which is hard for me to admit because I've always prided myself on being a very capable, hands-on kind of guy. But this constant need to be doing something, to be in motion, it's really starting to catch up with me in ways I never anticipated. 

At work, for instance. I mentioned I'm a special ed teacher, and a lot of what I do involves co-teaching or collaborating with other staff members. And apparently, my... my energy, I guess you could call it, has become a real problem. I've had colleagues complain that I'm overwhelming in the classroom. They say I'm always pacing, always jumping in before they finish a sentence, always rearranging things or hovering when they're trying to work one-on-one with a student. It got to the point where a couple of the general ed teachers went to the principal about it. They said I was creating a chaotic environment, which broke my heart because I'm just trying to be involved and helpful. But the complaints got serious enough that administration actually put me on a corrective action plan. A corrective plan, at 58 years old! I have to have these weekly check-ins now about my "professional presence" and "classroom demeanor," and it's just humiliating. I feel like I'm damaging the trust I've built with my colleagues over the years, and they're looking at me like I'm a liability rather than a partner.

And it's not just at school, either. It's spilling over into my home life, which is... well, it's really stressing my marriage. My wife and I, we help take care of her elderly mother who lives with us. It's a lot of work, a lot of routine—medications, meals, getting her to appointments. And my wife recently sat me down and told me that I'm making it harder for everyone. She said that when I'm supposed to be helping, I'm just a whirlwind. I'll start making lunch, but then I'll see the mail needs sorting, so I start doing that, and then I'll notice a loose hinge on the cabinet and go get my tools, and meanwhile, her mother is just sitting there waiting for her soup. My wife told me she feels like she has to manage my energy on top of managing her mother's care, and that's just... it's an awful thing to hear from your spouse. 

I'm trying to help. I really am. In my head, I'm tackling all these tasks that need to be done, I'm being productive, I'm keeping the household running. But the reality is, I'm exhausting the people around me. My wife is frustrated, my colleagues are annoyed, and I just feel this terrible guilt because I can't seem to just dial it back. I want to be a supportive husband and a reliable teacher, but this... this engine inside me just won't shut off, and it's really starting to fray my relationships.
Have you always been this way, even as a child?

Oh, absolutely. Yes. Without a doubt. I mean, it's really important to me that you understand this isn't just... it's not just some reaction to recent stress, you know? Like, it's not something that just started happening with this big family change, with my mother-in-law moving in and all the extra caretaking responsibilities that my wife and I are juggling now. No, no, no. This has been me since day one. 

My mother, she actually used to have this running joke about me when I was just a little guy in elementary school. She'd go to the parent-teacher conferences and come back and tell everyone that I practically taught the class from my seat. Though, honestly, I say "from my seat," but the reality was I was almost never actually sitting in it! I was always up, always wandering around the room, talking to the kids next to me, or—and this sounds exactly like what I do now with my co-teachers, which is tough to think about—but I was always cutting in before the teacher even finished giving directions. 

Like, she’d be halfway through explaining a math worksheet or a spelling assignment, and I’d already be blurting out the next step or talking over her because I just... I couldn't hold it in. I was just so eager to get to the doing part. I'd be out of my chair, leaning over someone else's desk, just constantly engaged, constantly in motion. 

So, yeah, this... this constant energy, this way of being, it was a fundamental part of who I was long, long before adulthood. It's literally the story of my life. I remember even into middle school and high school, it was the exact same thing. Always the kid who couldn't just sit quietly and listen. It’s just... it’s always been this way. I’ve always had this motor running, always had to be in the mix. So, no, it's definitely not a new development or some mid-life crisis thing. It's just how I've been wired my entire life.
Have you ever felt like your need to be constantly active and moving has significantly interfered with your ability to function effectively in your daily life or relationships?

Well, yeah, I mean... like I was just pouring my heart out about a minute ago, it really, really has. I mean, "significantly" is probably the exact right word for it, unfortunately. 

It’s just like I was saying about work. That corrective action plan I mentioned? That's not just a casual slap on the wrist. That’s a formal process. It goes in your file, you know? It means I have to sit down every single week with administration and have someone essentially grade my ability to just... be in a room with other professionals. And the worst part of it, the part that honestly just eats at me, is that I feel like I'm completely damaging the trust I’ve built with my colleagues over the years. I've worked with some of these general ed teachers for a decade, and now they look at me like I'm a bull in a china shop. Like I'm a liability instead of a co-teacher. And I'm just trying to help! I see a situation, I want to fix it, but now I’m realizing that my way of helping is actually tearing down those professional relationships. 

And then I go home, and it's the exact same story. Like I told you, with my mother-in-law living with us, the caregiving routine is incredibly demanding. It's a tight schedule of pills and meals and mobility help. And my wife... she flat out told me that I make those routines harder. She actually said that people have to manage my energy on top of everything else. Manage my energy! Like I'm one of the kids in my classroom, you know? 

It just breaks my heart because I’m trying so hard to be useful. I’m fixing things around the house, I’m moving around, I’m trying to take the load off her shoulders by doing ten things at once, but instead, I’m just exhausting her. I'm exhausting everybody. So, yes, to answer your question, it is absolutely interfering. It’s interfering with my ability to do my job, it's interfering with my marriage... I just feel like I'm eroding all this trust with my family and my coworkers, even though my only intention in the world is to help them.
Do you feel like your constant need to be active and moving is causing you a lot of personal distress?

Distress? Oh, God, yes. I mean, distress is almost putting it mildly at this point. It's... it's a heavy, heavy weight that I feel like I'm carrying around from the minute I wake up to the minute I finally manage to fall asleep. 

You know, I wake up every morning, and I have these really great intentions. I sit on the edge of the bed and I tell myself, "Okay, today, I'm going to be calm. Today, I'm just going to listen to my co-teachers, I'm going to let my wife handle her mother's breakfast without jumping in and making a mess of the routine." But then the day actually starts, and it's like this switch flips inside my chest, and I'm just going and going and going. I can't stop it. 

And then, at the end of the day, when the house finally quiets down... that's when the distress really hits me the hardest. I'll sit there in my favorite chair in the living room, usually after my wife has already gone to bed because she's just so totally exhausted from dealing with her mom and, frankly, dealing with me. And I just sit there in the quiet and replay the whole day in my head. I think about the looks on the other teachers' faces—you know, that tight-lipped, forced smile they give me when I've interrupted them for the fourth time in a single hour. Or I think about the heavy sigh my wife lets out when she walks into the kitchen and sees I've left a trail of half-finished chores everywhere because I got distracted trying to fix a squeaky floorboard. 

It brings on this profound sense of... of failure, really. Because I'm 58 years old! I should have all of this figured out by now, shouldn't I? I should be the wise, steady senior teacher at school. I should be the rock-solid, dependable husband at home. But instead, I feel like I'm this chaotic force of nature that everyone just has to brace themselves against. It makes me feel incredibly guilty. And honestly, sometimes it makes me feel really, really lonely, even when I'm surrounded by people all day long, because I can literally see them pulling away from me, bracing themselves when I walk into a room. 

So, yes, the distress is... it's very real. It's with me all the time lately. It just completely wears you down, feeling like your very nature, the core of who you are and how you operate, is a burden to the people you care about most in this world.
Have you experienced these feelings of constant activity and restlessness consistently throughout your adult life, or have there been periods where they were less pronounced?

Well, to be completely clear... the energy itself, the feeling of having a motor running inside me, that has absolutely always been there, just like I was saying before. But this... this absolute trainwreck of a situation where it's actually ruining my life and making everyone around me miserable? This specific level of trouble hasn't been forever. 

This level of trouble has been going on for about eight months now. It started exactly when our older relative—my wife's mother—moved in with us. 

Before that, I mean, sure, I was always the guy who couldn't sit still through a faculty meeting, and my wife would definitely roll her eyes when I’d start reorganizing the garage at ten o'clock at night. But we had a rhythm, you know? We had a system that worked for us for decades. I had my outlets. If I was feeling restless, I could just go for a long drive, or I'd stay late at the school setting up the classroom, or I'd just putter around the yard where I wasn't really in anyone's way. The activity was there, but it wasn't... it wasn't a destructive force. 

But then eight months ago, she moves in, and suddenly the whole dynamic of our lives completely flipped upside down. Suddenly the house is full. We had to turn the downstairs den into her bedroom, so my space to just pace around is gone. There's a strict schedule for her medications, her meals, her physical therapy exercises. And all of a sudden, my usual way of operating—my constant moving and fixing and just instinctively jumping into the middle of things—it just violently collided with this incredibly fragile, high-stress ecosystem we had to build for her. 

So when you ask if it's always been this pronounced... the restlessness is lifelong, yes, but the consequences? The sheer disaster of it all? That is a solid eight months of just pure chaos. It's like the extra pressure of her moving in just took all my usual quirks and magnified them into this massive problem that I suddenly can't control anymore, no matter how hard I try.
Did you exhibit these behaviors of constant activity and restlessness as a child, before the age of 12?

Oh, absolutely. Yes. I mean, without a doubt. It’s funny you ask about being a kid, because... well, I was just thinking about my mom the other day, actually, and how she used to handle me. 

My mother, she used to have this running joke about me when I was in elementary school. Like, second, third, fourth grade, right in that exact window you're asking about. She used to tell everyone that I essentially taught the class from my seat. And she didn't mean that I was, you know, some child prodigy or the teacher's pet or anything like that. She meant it because I was just... I was constantly out of my chair. I’d be up pacing the aisles, or leaning over someone else's desk, just talking and talking. 

I remember my third-grade teacher would start giving us instructions for an assignment, and I would just cut right in before she even finished her directions. I'd be blurting out what we were supposed to do next, just totally taking over, jumping the gun because I couldn't bear to just sit there and wait for her to get to the end of her sentence. 

So, yeah, it wasn't just a phase or something that developed later. I mean, looking back at it now, especially with what I do for a living in special ed, it’s so incredibly clear to me. This constant motor, this need to be in the middle of everything and moving around... it was just part of who I was long before adulthood. 

I really want to make sure I'm being clear about that, because I know I just went on and on about the last eight months and how awful it's been at the house. But this restlessness? It is absolutely not something that just started with this family change. The family change just... it just trapped all that energy in a much smaller, much more stressful box, if that makes sense. But the energy itself was always there. I was definitely that kid who couldn't stay in his seat for five minutes to save his life.
Have you experienced these feelings of constant activity and restlessness in multiple settings, such as at work, at home, and in social situations?

Oh, everywhere. Yes. It’s... well, it’s certainly not confined to just one place, I can tell you that for free. It’s not like I walk out my front door and suddenly I'm this calm, collected, zen-like person. I really, really wish it worked like that, but it bleeds into literally every single aspect of my life right now. 

Take work, for example. I mean, I’ve been at this school for years. I know the staff, I know the kids, I know the whole system inside and out. But lately, the complaints from the other teachers... I mentioned earlier about how I interrupt them, right? Well, it hasn't just been a few annoyed looks anymore. It’s gotten serious enough that administration actually had to step in. Me, a 58-year-old senior teacher, and they pulled me into the principal's office like I was some misbehaving middle schooler. They actually put me on a formal corrective plan. A corrective plan! Just because I can't stop pacing around the room during co-teaching blocks, and I'm constantly talking over the primary instructors. I just feel this immense, uncontrollable need to jump in and fix the lesson right then and there, but to them, I'm just completely steamrolling the whole curriculum. 

And then I come home, right? I come home hoping things will be a little more grounded, but it's just as bad there, if not worse. I try to help my wife with her mom. I really, really do. I want to be useful. But my wife actually sat me down recently, looking just completely bone-tired, and she told me that my "helping" is actually making all the caregiving routines harder. She said—and this really, really stung to hear—she said that on top of managing her mother's medications and her physical therapy and her meals, she feels like she has to manage *my* energy, too. Like I'm just this extra unpredictable element she has to wrangle. If I see her getting her mom's lunch ready, I'll just swoop in and take over because she's not moving fast enough for my brain, and then I end up dropping something, and then I'm frantically trying to mop the floor while simultaneously trying to fix a loose hinge on the cabinet... it just creates total chaos. 

It’s devastating, honestly. Because my intentions are good! I am genuinely trying to help keep everything moving and fixed and solved. But the reality is, I feel like I'm just actively damaging the trust I have with my colleagues and my family. They don't trust me to just be a steady, reliable presence anymore. So, yes, work, home, anywhere I go... it doesn't matter where I am. The fallout is just following me everywhere.
Did you exhibit these behaviors of constant activity and restlessness before the age of 7?

Before seven? Gosh, um... to be perfectly honest with you, going back quite that far... that's really stretching the limits of my memory. I mean, I'm fifty-eight years old, so we're talking about over half a century ago. When I try to think about early, early childhood, like kindergarten or preschool, it's all just these very blurry, disconnected little snapshots, you know? I don't have a continuous narrative in my head of how I acted day-to-day when I was five or six. 

Like I was saying just a minute ago, the stories my mom always told, the ones that really stuck with me, were mostly from second and third grade. That's when I was around eight or nine. I think that's probably because that's when the school really started paying attention and bringing it up to her, because the academic expectations shifted, you know, you actually had to sit at a desk and do worksheets. But before seven? I mean, I can only assume I was a total handful. I absolutely cannot imagine I was just sitting quietly in a corner doing puzzles while the other kids ran around. Knowing how my brain works, I was probably tearing through the house, but I just... I don't have any concrete stories to give you from that specific age. 

My parents just never really talked about my toddler or preschool years in that way. They mostly focused on the older school years because that's when the teachers started getting visibly frustrated with me and it became an actual issue they had to deal with at parent-teacher conferences. So, if you need a definitive yes or no about what I was like at age five or six... I just couldn't tell you for sure. It's mostly a blank spot. I really wish I had a better answer for you, because I want to make sure I'm giving you the complete picture of everything, but going back before age seven is just... it's just lost to time for me, I'm afraid.
Do you often interrupt others or blurt out answers before they finish speaking?

Oh, constantly. I know I touched on this a bit just a minute ago when I was talking about the issues at work, but it really is... it's a massive, massive issue for me right now. I just can't seem to stop myself. I keep jumping into conversations that I'm not even necessarily a part of. 

Like at school, for instance. If I'm in the hallway or the office and I hear my colleagues talking to each other, or even worse, if they're in the middle of talking to parents about a student's progress or an IEP... I just dive right in. I genuinely think I’m helping! I really do. My brain just goes, "Oh, I know how to fix this, I have the answer right here," and before I can even hit the brakes or think about social cues, I'm blurting it out. I end up completely talking over them before they’ve even had a chance to finish their sentence. 

And it’s the exact same story at home. I’ll hear my spouse talking to our relative—her mom—trying to sort out something about her care or her daily routine, and I just cannot just stand there and listen quietly. I interject, I swoop in, and I completely take charge of the whole conversation. I try to speed things along because I think I'm being this great, efficient problem-solver for them. But the reality is, I'm just intruding. I don't let either of them finish a single thought. 

It’s like this actual, physical pressure builds up in my chest if I have to wait my turn to speak, so I just... I just explode with whatever I want to say. I'm constantly taking over before anyone else has made their point. And it’s awful, because they just feel like I don't respect what they have to say, when really my intentions are purely to help... it's just that my mouth moves a hundred miles an hour faster than my ability to wait.
Have your symptoms of restlessness and constant activity caused significant problems in your relationships or work performance before you turned 12 years old?

Oh, absolutely. Like I mentioned a few minutes ago, those elementary school years—second, third, fourth grade, right in that window before I turned twelve—that's when it really became a huge, undeniable issue. 

My mother... well, my mother had this joke she used to tell everyone, even years later at family gatherings. She used to joke that even in elementary school, I taught the class from my seat. Or, well, I suppose I should say *not* from my seat, because that was the whole problem! I just couldn't contain myself. I was always, and I mean *always*, out of my chair. The teacher would be up at the front of the room, trying to explain an assignment or hand out papers, and I’d be up, wandering around, talking to my neighbors, or I'd be cutting in and shouting out the next step before the teacher had even finished giving the directions. It drove them absolutely up the wall, as you can imagine. I spent so much time getting reprimanded or having notes sent home because I was just completely disrupting the flow of the entire classroom. 

So, I really want to make sure I'm clear about this, because I think it's an important distinction to make. This behavior, this constant need to move and intervene and talk over people... this was part of who I was long, long before adulthood. I know we've talked a lot today about my wife and her mom, and how chaotic things are at the house right now with all the medical routines, but I need you to know that this isn't just some stress reaction that just started with this recent family change. This isn't just caregiver burnout or me reacting to a stressful mid-life situation. It’s been my normal for half a century. The problems I'm having at work with the administration and at home with my wife right now... they're really just the adult version of me being eight years old and driving my teachers crazy because I couldn't just sit still and listen.
Have you experienced these feelings of constant activity and restlessness in every setting you've been in, consistently, over the years?

Well, let me clarify that a little bit, because I know I just sat here and told you that this isn't just a stress reaction to my current life, and I stand by that. The core of who I am, that constant need to move and do things, that has absolutely been there my whole life. But if you're asking if it's been *this* intense, this consistently disruptive in literally every single setting all day long? No, not quite like this. 

This specific level of trouble—where I feel like I'm just buzzing out of my skin from the second I wake up until the second I try to force myself to sleep, where I'm completely blowing up conversations at work and at home—that has really been going on for about eight months now. 

It started right around the time our older relative—my wife's mother—moved in with us. And, I mean, you have to understand, when you bring an elderly parent into your home, it just completely upends the entire ecosystem of the house. Suddenly there are all these new schedules, the medical equipment, the constant coordinating of care, and my wife is understandably stressed to the max. So I try to step in, my brain goes into this hyper-drive trying to manage and fix every little thing, and it's like the dial just got turned all the way up to maximum and then the knob snapped off. 

So for the last eight months, it's just been this relentless, non-stop motor running inside me at an entirely new speed. I take that frantic energy from the house, I carry it with me into the school building, I drive my colleagues crazy, and then I bring it right back home. So, yes, the restlessness is a lifelong companion, but this absolute peak, this unmanageable level of constant trouble across every single area of my life? That's been a solid eight months, ever since she moved into the spare bedroom. It's just amplified everything I already struggled with by a factor of ten.
Can you recall any instances from before you were 7 years old where you exhibited restless or overly active behavior?

Before I was seven? Gosh, I mean, you're asking me to go back... well, over fifty years now. I'm fifty-eight, so we're talking about, what, 1970? 1971? It's really tough to say. I know I just went on and on about second and third grade, which would be right around that seven or eight-year-old mark, and those memories are crystal clear because of all the trouble I got into and the notes sent home. But before seven? Like kindergarten, or preschool age? I honestly... I just draw a blank. 

I mean, logically, if I was jumping out of my seat at age eight, I can't imagine I was a perfect little angel sitting perfectly still at age five. But as for actual, specific instances? I really just don't have them. My mom passed a while back, so I can't exactly call her up and ask if I was bouncing out of my crib or running laps around the living room as a toddler. I wish I could give you a specific story, like driving a kindergarten teacher crazy or something, but it's just a fog that far back. 

I really only start remembering the constant moving and the reprimands once I hit about second grade, when the school structure got more rigid, you know? When you're in kindergarten, they kind of expect kids to be a little squirmy and active, so maybe it just didn't register as a huge problem yet, or maybe it did and I just didn't retain the memory of it. But yeah, to answer your question, before seven, I just don't have any concrete examples for you at all. I just can't remember.
Did you exhibit any symptoms of restlessness or excessive activity before you were 12 years old?

Well, yes, absolutely. I know we touched on this a few minutes ago, but it's really important to me that you understand this isn't some new development. It’s not just the stress of my mother-in-law moving in, or the medical equipment, or the chaotic schedules we're dealing with right now. This is... well, this is just who I am, and who I've always been, long before I was an adult with a mortgage and a career in special education. 

I mean, if we go back to elementary school, before I turned twelve, it was already a massive issue. My mother—God rest her soul—she had this running joke. She'd tell everyone, at Thanksgiving, at family reunions, you name it. She used to joke that even in elementary school, I taught the class from my seat. Except, of course, the punchline was always that I was *never* actually in my seat! I was constantly up, out of my chair, wandering the aisles. The teacher would be up front, you know, trying to hand out a worksheet or explain a math problem, and I’d just be roaming around, talking to my friends, or I'd be shouting out the answers or the next step of the directions before the teacher even had a chance to finish her sentence. I just couldn't hold it in. I couldn't just sit there and wait my turn.
